title: Level 2 Biology — Life Processes at the Cellular Level (2024)
subject: biology

questions.text: Write the word equation or the chemical equation for aerobic respiration.
questions.expectedAnswer: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy / ATP.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correct word equation (glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy / ATP) or correct non-balanced/balanced symbol equation, or a mixture of symbol and word equation. Accept adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

questions.text:
The peregrine falcon (Falco peregrinus) is found across much of the world, including parts of New Zealand. It is a swift and agile predator capable of reaching speeds above 320 km/h during hunting dives called stoops. Peregrine falcons inhabit cliffs, open country, and even city buildings across their range.

Their exceptional eyesight allows them to spot prey from altitude, and they rely on explosive speed to strike small birds mid-flight. During cruising flight between hunting attempts, they glide at around 50 km/h, conserving energy while scanning for targets.

Peregrine falcons possess highly efficient cardiovascular systems, which deliver oxygen rapidly during high-speed pursuits.

Discuss the processes of anaerobic and aerobic respiration, linking them to the activities of the peregrine falcon.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- the processes of anaerobic respiration and aerobic respiration in the peregrine falcon, including where in the cell each form of respiration takes place
- why the peregrine falcon can only sustain anaerobic respiration for short periods during a high-speed stoop
- the advantages and disadvantages associated with the peregrine falcon using both anaerobic and aerobic respiration.
questions.expectedAnswer: Anaerobic respiration occurs in the cytoplasm and produces ATP quickly but inefficiently (2 ATP per glucose). Aerobic respiration occurs in the mitochondria and produces up to 38 ATP per glucose but requires oxygen. During a high-speed stoop, the falcon's muscles demand energy faster than oxygen can be delivered, so anaerobic respiration supplements energy production.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved (A3-A4): Describes aerobic respiration AND anaerobic respiration; where aerobic respiration (cytoplasm AND mitochondria) takes place; an advantage of anaerobic respiration; both types of respiration are useful because they work with each other; a disadvantage of anaerobic respiration; a disadvantage of aerobic respiration. Merit (M5-M6): Explains anaerobic respiration making links to the role of O2 being absent and the location in cells; an advantage of anaerobic respiration; a disadvantage; an advantage of aerobic respiration; a disadvantage; why there is a need for both systems/forms of respiration. Excellence (E7-E8): Discusses where and when anaerobic and aerobic respiration occurs, making links to when the falcon is diving/stooping vs cruising/soaring; the advantages and disadvantages of aerobic and anaerobic respiration to the falcon.

questions.text: Name three key structures found within a chloroplast and briefly describe the function of each.
questions.expectedAnswer: 1. Thylakoid membrane / granum — site of the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis. 2. Stroma — site of the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle). 3. Outer membrane — controls what enters and leaves the chloroplast.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Three structures correctly named with brief function. Structures include: outer membrane, inner membrane, stroma, thylakoid/granum, and lamella/thylakoid membrane.

questions.text:
Some plants that grow in exposed alpine areas of New Zealand are known as 'cushion plants'. These plants are typically compact and dome-shaped with thick, leathery leaves and reduced leaf surface area. Plants growing in sheltered lowland podocarp forests, referred to as 'canopy ferns', tend to have larger, thinner fronds.

Cushion plants tend to have smaller chloroplasts but a higher concentration of chlorophyll per chloroplast compared to canopy ferns. Despite receiving intense direct sunlight, cushion plants face freezing temperatures, drying winds, and thin soils that drain quickly.

Canopy ferns in sheltered forests receive less intense, filtered sunlight but benefit from consistently moist soils and protection from wind.

With reference to the information above, evaluate how leaf structure, and the size and concentration of chloroplasts within plant cells, can be influenced by environmental conditions.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- the process of photosynthesis, describing its key stages
- the correlation between the size and chlorophyll concentration of chloroplasts in cushion plants and canopy ferns, and how these differences relate to photosynthesis
- why cushion plants tend to lose less water through transpiration than canopy ferns, despite being exposed to more wind and sunlight.
questions.expectedAnswer: Photosynthesis occurs in two stages: the light-dependent phase in the thylakoid membranes and the light-independent phase (Calvin cycle) in the stroma. Cushion plants have smaller but more concentrated chloroplasts to maximise light capture in harsh conditions. Their compact leaves with thick cuticles and fewer stomata reduce water loss.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved (A3-A4): The process of photosynthesis; part of the light-dependent reaction; part of the light-independent reaction; the light-dependent phase as occurring in the thylakoid/grana; the light-independent phase as occurring in the stroma; the difference in environmental conditions between cushion plants and canopy ferns; that differences in chloroplast size/concentration affect photosynthesis rate; stomata function/location. Merit (M5-M6): Explains the light-dependent phase and where it occurs; the light-independent phase and where it occurs; why cushion plants have smaller chloroplasts with concentrated chlorophyll; why canopy ferns have larger, thinner fronds; how/why water loss differs between cushion plants and canopy ferns. Excellence (E7-E8): Discusses the key phases of photosynthesis and why environmental factors are important; cushion vs canopy plants with respect to their chloroplast characteristics, linking to photosynthesis; the difference in water loss rates for cushion plants and canopy ferns, making comparisons and contrasts.

questions.text:
All living organisms are composed of cells that must maintain a balance between their internal and external environments to function properly.

Evaluate the impact of changes in the surface area to volume ratio on the process of diffusion, and why changes in this ratio may trigger cell division.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- the process of diffusion and its role in cellular activities
- how and why the surface area to volume ratio changes as a cell grows
- how the surface area to volume ratio influences the movement of substances into and out of the cell
- the relationship between the surface area to volume ratio, diffusion, and the initiation of cell division, giving examples of when cell division rates are high in both plants and animals.
questions.expectedAnswer: Diffusion is the passive movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so the SA:Vol ratio decreases.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved (A3-A4): Describes the process of diffusion as the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration; diffusion as a passive process requiring no energy; that diffusion occurs across a semi-permeable membrane and is involved in gas exchange in cells; a way that SA:Vol ratio changes (cell growth/division); that smaller cells/cells with higher SA:Vol ratio have more effective transport OR that larger cells/cells that have lower SA:Vol ratio have less effective transport; an example of high cell division rate in an animal/plant. Merit (M5-M6): Explains the purpose of diffusion; changes to the SA:Vol ratio as a cell grows; why SA:Vol ratio affects the movement of substances into/out of a cell; why cells must divide once they reach a certain size; an example of cell type/system linked to cell division rates/diffusion. Excellence (E7-E8): Discusses the proper functioning of cells, showing linked ideas; effective transport of substances into/out of cells; smaller SA:Vol ratios are not effective at maintaining exchange; appropriate examples of high cell division rates, including animal/plant examples to support their discussion.
